newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Ousted Zairean president Mobutu arrives in Morocco.
newsitem.headline: Ousted Zairean president Mobutu arrives in Morocco.

text.p: Ousted Zairean president Mobutu Sese Seko and his family were staying in the Moroccan capital Rabat on Sunday after arriving aboard three Gabonese aircraft, a senior Moroccan security official said.
"Mobutu and his family arrived aboard three airplanes discreetly in the Rabat military airport. Mobutu and his family will stay at the 50-room Amphitrite hotel," the official told Reuters.
The hotel is situated some 20 km (12 miles) south of Rabat on the Atlantic coast close to the royal palace of Skhirat.
"Three Gabonese aircraft transported Mobutu and his family to the Rabat military airport thanks to the cooperation of Moroccan authorities," said the official.
He said Mobutu arrived late on Saturday night but could not say how long the former Zairean leader would be staying in Morocco.
"Mobutu and his family are expected to move later to the southern city of Marrakesh," the official said.
He declined to give any further details but a reliable source told Reuters that work had been under way at a luxury villa in Marrakesh in preparation for Mobutu.
Reporters, photographers and television crews had been waiting for Mobutu to arrive at Rabat's civilian airport.
Earlier, a Reuters correspondent saw an unusual deployment of security forces around the Amphitrite hotel.
"The hotel was booked for Mobutu and his family... Therefore it is now not open to the public," said a Moroccan official.

The hotel is near a clean and beautiful Atlantic beach and is close to the highway linking the Moroccan business centre of Casablanca to the political capital of Rabat, where Morocco's King Hassan II lives.
The king met Mobutu in February when the Zairean leader stopped in Rabat on his way home to Zaire from Europe.
Morocco sent troops to Zaire to help put down a 1977 secessionist uprising in Shaba province after Zairean forces were overwhelmed.
Moroccan troops relieved French and Belgian paratroopers who backed Zairean authorities in halting an uprising in the Kolwezi area the following year.
Laurent Kabila and his rebels proclaimed victory in Zaire's seven-month civil war on Saturday and purged Africa's third largest nation of one of the more obvious symbols of Mobutu's rule -- its name.

Kabila, 56, declared himself head of state in a statement he read at his headquarters in the southern mining city of Lubumbashi as his forces moved into the capital Kinshasa virtually unopposed to the cheers of jubilant residents.
"Mr Laurent Desire Kabila assumes from today the functions of the head of state of the Democratic Republic of the Congo," the statement said.
This was the name Zaire had on independence from Belgium in 1960 until Mobutu changed it in 1971.

Sporadic exchanges of mortar and automatic weapons fire were heard at nightfall in Kinshasa and reports of shootouts with diehard Mobutu loyalists suggested the rebels still had to consolidate their hold over the city of five million people.
Mobutu, 66 and suffering from cancer, seized power in 1965 and proved one of Africa's most enduring strongmen. Western powers supported him as a Cold War bastion against Soviet communism.

Critics denounced him as everything from a dictator to a thief and accused him of plundering what is potentially one of Africa's richest countries and amassing a huge personal fortune while his people struggled against poverty and neglect.
Mobutu refused to resign as head of state, as demanded by Kabila, but his abrupt departure from the capital on Friday triggered intense speculation that he was on his way to exile.
Switzerland, sensitive to accusations that it handled dirty money, has frozen all the Mobutu family assets in its banks and on its territory.
